articles.title_orig: An EU approach to managing China’s cleantech dominance
articles.title_zh: An EU approach to managing China’s cleantech dominance
articles.content_orig:
Europe will remain deeply intertwined with China, and slowing the energy transition would do little to change that. But only some of Europe’s dependencies on Chinese clean technology create strategic vulnerability, and the political debate rarely distinguishes them. The EU needs a policy of differentiated de-risking: one that assumes neither reciprocity nor benign intent from Beijing, matches its response to the type of dependency at stake, protects the control layers of its energy system first and uses the leverage it already holds.
Europe relies heavily on China across clean technology. More than 97% of solar panels deployed in Europe are imported, mainly from China. Chinese manufacturers have supplied around 70% of the solar inverters installed in Europe, and China provides about 98% of the EU’s rare-earth permanent magnets .
But similar reliance does not mean similar risk. A solar panel is largely passive once installed. Magnets carry supply risk: Chinese export restrictions on rare earths and permanent magnets in 2025 shut down several European car production lines while firms waited for export licences. Inverters carry control risk: they stay connected after installation, and Huawei and Sungrow alone have remote access capabilities linked to 168 GW of European PV capacity.
Europe’s toolbox is growing. The EU–China agreements of October 2026 on hybrid vehicles and rare-earth licensing show de-risking turning into safeguards, quotas and licensing rules, alongside trade defence, investment screening and cybersecurity requirements.
What is missing is a clear logic for deciding which tool to use where. Without one, the most pressing concern or the loudest political voice of the moment will decide, weakening Europe’s position towards China and towards the partners it needs to build alternatives.
In our briefing, we introduce two risk ladders: one for energy-system security and one for industrial capability. Some dependencies matter on one ladder but not the other; some, such as inverters, sit high on both. Together, the ladders underpin eight principles for managing Europe’s cleantech interdependence with China.

articles.title_orig: Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention
articles.title_zh: Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention
articles.content_orig:
The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill .
“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X .
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”
“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.
“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.
“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.
The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang , the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”
But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”
“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”
“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said .
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.
“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.
“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”
“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.
Brennan Leach is an associate producer for NBC News covering the Senate.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq futures turn lower after Nvidia rally as Jensen Huang returns: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq futures turn lower after Nvidia rally as Jensen Huang returns: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Major tech stocks rebounded across the board Monday, sharply reversing Friday's steep sell-off when artificial intelligence stocks fell in the Nasdaq's worst week since 2020.
Shares of Nvidia surged 31.48% after the company announced Monday morning that Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO . The semiconductor giant gained back nearly $1 trillion in market cap, posting its best day since May 2003.
Nvidia's surge and Huang's reinstatement followed a more than 40% slump in the stock over the past month. The company has been embattled as reports surfaced about Huang's multiple extramarital affairs — one of which was with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang resigned as CEO of the company he founded on Nov. 12.
The Nasdaq Composite surged 6.51% Monday, for its best day since April 9, 2025. The Nasdaq slid 10% last week, with tech stocks having a rocky week as investors remained nervous about the valuation of some AI companies and business models. All three major averages ended last week in correction territory, and the Nasdaq turned negative for 2026.
Shares of Big Tech companies and other stocks related to the AI trade saw a lift Monday on the Nvidia news.
Shares of Alphabet surged 6.34%, Meta gained 6.55%, Amazon jumped 3.47% and Microsoft increased 1.65%. SpaceX added 4.35%, Arm Holdings surged 16.08% and AMD added 6.85%. Dell and Micron posted some of the sector's biggest gains of the day, gaining 20.46% and 19.04%, respectively. The iShares Semiconductor ETF gained 13.63%.
Neoclouds, which have seen a particularly choppy few months amid AI boom financing concerns, surged on Huang's reinstatement. Nebius soared 20.28%, CoreWeave gained 22.32% and Iren gained 23.86%.
Following a brief premarket surge, Anthropic shares posted a decline of 1.43% in its third day of trading. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, before closing down 8.5% on Friday.
Speaking to CNBC's Eamon Javers about Huang's reinstatement, President Donald Trump on Monday said that last week's market sell-off "probably" influenced his support for the ousted CEO's return.
"Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about," Trump said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board directly and that he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang, who the president said "did nothing wrong."
"That thing's like a rocket ship going in the wrong direction. Now it's a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it's taking the whole market with it," Trump said, referring to Nvidia's stock price.
"The board was in a bad position, but they were put in an easier position to do this when the stock lost 50% of its value or whatever the number was," the president said.

articles.title_orig: Sanofi strikes $41bn deal to buy US biotech Insmed
articles.title_zh: Sanofi strikes $41bn deal to buy US biotech Insmed
articles.content_orig:
BRIDGEWATER, N.J. , Nov. 24, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Sanofi today announced an agreement to acquire Insmed (Nasdaq: INSM), a publicly traded, U.S.-based global biopharmaceutical company with two commercialized medicines and a promising, innovative pipeline. The transaction is intended to broaden Sanofi's presence in respiratory diseases, where significant unmet patient need remains.
The acquisition includes BRINSUPRI ® (brensocatib) and ARIKAYCE ® (amikacin liposome inhalation suspension), along with a differentiated, phase 3 clinical program, treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder (TPIP), which has potential across multiple rare respiratory diseases. The acquisition also brings promising earlier-stage programs and research capabilities across immunology and rare diseases, reinforcing Sanofi's own innovation and immunology capabilities globally.
Insmed is a compelling strategic fit, building on Sanofi's longstanding experience in immunology and rare diseases. Combining Insmed's highly differentiated portfolio and scientific expertise with Sanofi's global reach is expected to expand patient access to important respiratory medicines while augmenting Sanofi's commercial leadership and rebuild of its pipeline.
This acquisition is expected to improve Sanofi's financial profile over the mid- and long-term and expand the company's portfolio in core focus areas.
"I am delighted to welcome Insmed to Sanofi. This acquisition is a major strategic step to significantly accelerate our mid- and long-term growth trajectory and further strengthen our mid- and early-stage pipeline," said Belen Garijo, Chief Executive Officer of Sanofi. "Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success. Together, we have the opportunity to build on these achievements, reach more patients globally and reinforce our leadership in diseases of significant unmet medical need. This acquisition is another example of how we are executing on our strategic roadmap with momentum to drive Sanofi's next phase of growth."
"The Insmed team has always set out to change what is possible for patients. In just over a year since launch, we made BRINSUPRI the standard of care for NCFB patients, while continuing to advance our commercial portfolio and Phase 3 pipeline with a combined multibillion-dollar peak sales potential," said Will Lewis, Chair and Chief Executive Officer of Insmed. "This transaction delivers immediate, certain cash value for Insmed shareholders and ensures the momentum we have built continues. In Sanofi, we have a partner that recognizes the value of our science, commercial execution, and the exceptional culture we have created. Together, we expect to bring our therapies to more patients around the world, faster than we ever could on our own."
BRINSUPRI is a small molecule, once-daily, oral, reversible inhibitor of dipeptidyl peptidase 1 (DPP1), approved in the U.S., EU, UK and Japan for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB), with the indicated patient populations varying by jurisdiction. BRINSUPRI is the first and only approved treatment for NCFB and a first-in-class DPP1 inhibitor targeting neutrophilic inflammation. Following its U.S. launch in August 2025, BRINSUPRI has already reached blockbuster status, delivering $1.09 billion in revenue through September 30, 2026, with substantial additional growth expected.
ARIKAYCE is an inhaled antibacterial treatment used in combination with multidrug therapy for certain adults with mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease and is the only approved inhaled therapy specifically indicated for treatment-refractory patients in the U.S., EU and Japan. ARIKAYCE revenues were $433.8 million in 2025, representing 19% annual growth. In addition, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in September accepted under priority review an application for ARIKAYCE for the treatment of MAC lung disease as part of a combination antibacterial drug regimen.
TPIP is a prostanoid being developed as a once-daily inhaled therapy for pulmonary hypertension and fibrotic lung disease. With once-daily dosing and the potential for multiple rare respiratory indications, TPIP could become a significant growth driver for Sanofi beyond 2030, subject to successful clinical development, regulatory approvals, and commercial execution.
Transaction Terms and Financial Considerations
Under the terms of the merger agreement, Sanofi will acquire all outstanding shares of Insmed for $175 per share in cash, reflecting a total equity value of approximately $41.0 billion (€37.6 billion). The consideration represents a premium of approximately 46% to Insmed's unaffected closing share price on November 18, 2026, the day prior to media reports of a possible transaction.
The transaction is expected to strengthen Sanofi's mid- to long-term growth profile. The transaction is expected to be accretive to Sanofi's business earnings per share (EPS) by the end of 2028.
Sanofi is funding the acquisition through a combination of debt financing and cash on hand, and has secured committed financing in support of the transaction. Sanofi will maintain its conservative financial policy. The combined group's anticipated cash generation is expected to support rapid deleveraging, while retaining flexibility to invest in early-stage BD/M&A opportunities. Sanofi remains committed to its capital allocation policy, including its progressive dividend, and expects to maintain a strong credit rating.
The transaction has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies.
The closing of the transaction is subject to approval by Insmed shareholders, receipt of U.S. and certain non-U.S. regulatory approvals and other customary conditions.
Subject to the satisfaction or waiver of these conditions, the transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027.
The proposed acquisition is not expected to have any impact on Sanofi's financial guidance for 2026.
Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC is acting as exclusive financial advisor to Insmed, and Freshfields LLP is acting as legal advisor to Insmed. Cooley LLP and Hunton Andrews Kurth LLP are also acting as legal advisors to Insmed. Collected Strategies is serving as strategic communications advisor to Insmed.
J.P. Morgan is acting as exclusive financial advisor to Sanofi, and Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP is acting as legal advisor to Sanofi.
Conference Call for Investors and Analysts

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s Return as Nvidia CEO Changes US-China Chip Trade Outlook Overnight, Says BofA — But a Bigg
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s Return as Nvidia CEO Changes US-China Chip Trade Outlook Overnight, Says BofA — But a Bigg
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang and Donald Trump on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Eleven days. That’s how long it took Jensen Huang to return to his post of CEO of Nvidia after resigning in the wake of an alleged espionage scandal that rocked the business, tech, and policy worlds.
On Nov. 12, Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded in 1993 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected was a Chinese spy. Her former company, Megaspeed, is also under criminal investigation over possible export-control violations. (The two Huangs are not related.)
But on Monday, Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump personally claimed credit for the reversal, telling CNBC that “I convinced them” and “I made the deal.”
The stock market surged, with Nvidia shares rising more than 30% as trading opened Monday. The broader market has now recovered more than half of last week’s plunge, temporarily easing fears that an AI slump could lead to a recession.
But Nvidia and Huang still face an uncertain and treacherous path forward. Here are six big questions about his return.
Just a week ago, the NVIDIA board made it clear that it intended to turn the page on the Huang era. At the company’s Q3 earnings call on Nov. 17, chairman Harvey Jones told investors that the board did “not intend to reinstate Huang,” despite the fact that the former CEO was angling for a return.
The board had plenty of reasons to not want him back. Reuters reported that Huang had misled several company leaders about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Separate reports emerged alleging that Jensen Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported to him.
But the board also faced intense pressure to reinstate him. An online campaign attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including from executives like Elon Musk and people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees.
And most centrally, President Trump said Monday that he personally intervened. Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly,” and that Vice President JD Vance was also involved in discussions. On Monday morning, Trump indicated to a reporter that he knew Huang would be reinstated before the news broke.
Notably, the board reinstated Huang before completing its independent investigation. Directors said a series of meetings had satisfied them about Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that senior government officials had assuaged their national-security concerns. They did not identify those officials or explain what information they supplied.
The swift about-face has provoked questions even from Republicans. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” wrote Utah Senator John Curtis.
It remains unclear what U.S. intelligence discovered about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang—and how damaging its findings were. The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang remained in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through the fall of 2026—a period overlapping with her affair with Jensen Huang.
But the intelligence community has not publicly established that she knowingly acted as a spy, and Beijing has denied the allegation. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche did “not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
However, a slew of questions remains unanswered. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, said on Sunday that an investigation into Alice Huang and her firm Megaspeed was ongoing. And more reporting continues to be published about the complex relationships between Megaspeed, the Chinese government, and various Chinese AI companies. Bloomberg, for instance, reported that a company founded by Alice Huang procured Nvidia chips installed at a Shanghai data center connected to the Megaspeed network.
The Nvidia scandal has exacerbated deep fissures within the Trump administration over China. More laissez-faire members of the administration, exemplified by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are happy with Nvidia selling some of its chips to China, which they argue is good for U.S. business interests and keeping China hooked on American technology.
But the Nvidia scandal empowered a competing faction of China hawks, who argue that Trump should take a more adversarial stance. Four days after Huang resigned, the Commerce Department issued a rule intended to close a major loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access restricted American chips remotely through data centers in third countries.
With Huang back in charge at Nvidia, the balance could tip back in his favor.
The scandal has also revealed cracks within Nvidia, the world’s top chip supplier. It’s no secret that Huang has always been the culture-setter for Nvidia and its hard-charging, relentless work ethic. But recent reporting, especially from the Times , alleges that Huang crossed a line into public humiliation, threats, and verbal abuse.
Now that Huang is back, will his power be checked—or unleashed? The board, in its statement, stressed more oversight, including a new committee of independent directors that will oversee national-security and export-control risks, and a chief compliance officer who reports to a board committee.
But Huang has now survived a seemingly insurmountable crisis with the support of the president and other Silicon Valley power players. That could make him more difficult to restrain, in a manner similar to how Sam Altman returned to OpenAI with a reconstituted board that left him more powerful than before his ouster.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, an investment research company, says that the fact that Huang was reinstated before his investigation was concluded “is going to add to those corporate governance questions that investors have"—especially given that the company is "exposed to several material risks."
As Huang resumes the role of helming one of the biggest companies in the world, he will also be pulled away from his desk to Washington to answer questions from irate policymakers. He has agreed to a transcribed congressional interview on Dec. 1 before the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees, and has also been asked to appear on Dec. 3 in a public Senate hearing.
That scrutiny will likely increase in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Many Democratic candidates ran on platforms of accountability and rooting out corruption. Lawmakers have already demanded that the administration preserve records involving Nvidia, Megaspeed, Huang’s communications with Trump, and the government’s export-control decisions.
“Congress must get to the bottom of what’s going on at Nvidia. Jensen Huang must testify under oath,” Congressman Greg Casar wrote in a statement on Monday.
Investigators may also examine Trump’s financial interest in Nvidia. Public disclosures show that he bought between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock in the days before his administration rescinded a Biden-era chip rule in May 2025, and made at least three additional purchases shortly after announcing that Nvidia could sell H200 chips to China. White House representatives have stated that Trump’s holdings are managed by independent advisors.
Huang’s return stopped the stock market bleeding on Monday. Longterm, his presence could be enormously beneficial to an industry that critics feared was on the verge of bursting. Huang has long played the role of AI’s chief investor, salesman, and diplomat.

articles.title_orig: Chinese official sentenced to death for spying and leaking "top secret" information, state media reports
articles.title_zh: Chinese official sentenced to death for spying and leaking "top secret" information, state media reports
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country and leaking "top secret" information in return for payment, state-affiliated media reported.
The convicted man, identified only by the surname Ma, had been recruited by foreign intelligence while working abroad, according to a report on Monday in an online account run by Gold Wall Press, a publishing company linked to China's National Administration of State Secrets Protection.
The recruiter, identified only as "Kailin," met Ma frequently, originally on the pretext of learning Chinese.
"Kailin gradually shifted the focus of their discussions to politically sensitive topics," probing for China's operational and personnel details in another country, the report said, without specifying which countries were involved.
"Ma disclosed a large amount of sensitive information concerning China's institutions" in the unidentified country, it said.
Kailin later introduced Ma to a colleague, who threatened to report that he had leaked information to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.
Ma agreed to work for the foreign intelligence network and signed a cooperation agreement that included clauses on "confidentiality" and "loyalty."
He received monthly payments in exchange, and "a laptop for the purposes of sending and receiving intelligence," the report said.
Ma returned to China after he finished his overseas posting and "embarked on a long-term career of espionage."
"He would extract relevant content from classified documents and materials he came into contact with at work; in the evenings, after returning home, he would organize the information and send it via espionage websites," the report said.
Ma stole and leaked "over a hundred pieces of intelligence" during that period, it said, without specifying how, when or for how long that lasted.
He was "eventually apprehended" and a court found that he had received more than 1 million yuan ($150,000) in exchange for 35 pieces of information, some of which were "top secret," the report said.
The report did not specify when or where Ma was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.
"This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call," the report said.
"The tactics employed by espionage and intelligence agencies are becoming increasingly cunning" and included emotional manipulation and blackmail, it said.

articles.title_orig: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.title_zh: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.content_orig:
China's automotive transformation is creating a new set of industrial capabilities that could benefit the global automotive industry as a whole.
Over the past decade, China has developed a highly interconnected automotive ecosystem, bringing together battery technology, intelligent driving, vehicle software, advanced manufacturing, and an increasingly sophisticated supply chain.
The significance of this transformation lies not only in the competitiveness of Chinese automakers, but also in the opportunities these capabilities create for companies around the world.
Volkswagen offers an interesting example. The group is targeting annual exports of around 300,000 vehicles from China by 2030. More importantly, it plans to introduce China-developed vehicle platforms and electronic architecture into selected overseas markets，which represents a meaningful evolution in the role of China within multinational automakers' global operations.
Image source: Volkswagen Group China
For decades, international automotive companies brought technology, manufacturing expertise, management practices, and engineering capabilities to China. These contributions played an important role in the development of China's automotive industry.
Today, we are beginning to see industrial capabilities flow in the other direction as well.
Chinese companies are expanding their manufacturing, engineering, and supply-chain operations overseas. Meanwhile, multinational companies are increasingly integrating China's innovation resources into their global development strategies.
This is not simply a reversal of traditional globalization. It is an evolution toward a more interconnected model of industrial collaboration.
Different markets still have their own strengths. China's rapidly evolving technology ecosystem can complement Europe's engineering expertise, Japan's manufacturing and quality management capabilities, and the growing industrial capacity of emerging markets.
The opportunity is not to replicate the Chinese automotive model everywhere, but to combine complementary capabilities and develop solutions that meet different local needs.
Of course, this transformation brings challenges. Companies must navigate regulatory differences, cultural expectations, financial pressures, and increasingly complex localization requirements.
These challenges also highlight the importance of deeper industrial collaboration, local capability building, and disciplined long-term investment.
For global automotive executives, the strategic question should therefore extend beyond how to compete with Chinese companies. It should also be about how to leverage China's industrial capabilities, integrate them with existing strengths, and create better products and sustainable businesses for consumers around the world .
In my view, the greatest value of China's automotive transformation will not be measured solely by the number of vehicles Chinese companies sell globally. It will also be measured by how much this transformation contributes to the evolution of the entire global automotive industry.
That is a much greater opportunity than winning a car war.

articles.title_orig: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.title_zh: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: Pope Francis had visions of the Devil and Hell, diaries reveal
articles.title_zh: Pope Francis had visions of the Devil and Hell, diaries reveal
articles.content_orig:
Pope Francis suffered a spiritual crisis during his papacy in which he saw visions of the devil and hell while struggling with how to exercise power, newly published diaries of the late pontiff reveal.
The Argentine pope intermittently kept a diary between 1992 and 2024, first during his time as a bishop in Argentina and then following his election as pope. Now, several of those entries have been compiled in a book published on Tuesday. It was written by Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, one of Francis’ closest aides and a fellow Argentine, who offers a detailed commentary on the papal diaries.
The 160-page “The Private Diary of Pope Francis” is focused primarily on the pope’s spiritual life and pastoral agenda, although it also details how the first Latin American pope struggled with temptations connected to the use of power in 2021-2022. It also includes what the pope describes as encounters with the devil along with his thoughts about his successor, Leo XIV, whom he described as “irreproachable.”
The publication of papal diaries is rare, but not unprecedented, and can provide unusually personal insights. While some popes order that their personal papers be destroyed, the diaries of John XXIII were published posthumously, as were some papers of John Paul II.
Francis wrote 86 pages of the black-covered diary — initially a planner for the year 1992 — while he was in Argentina and 55 pages while he was pope. “He showed me a few books, including what looked like an old agenda book with a leather cover. When he opened it, I saw that it was filled with notes in his handwriting. He told me, ‘From this, you will all see,’” Fernández wrote.
Here are some of the major revelations:
The diaries say that the pope experienced “frequent demonic attacks,” and Francis details three encounters with the devil: two while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires and another in 2018, when he was pope. Francis wrote that the devil has “eyes of fire,” also describing them as “menacing” and “seductive” eyes.
“I can’t forget his eyes the first two times — from the car when I was returning to the house, and in the choir loft during Mass. However, he always reappears in different situations,” the pope wrote in an entry for August 18, 2024. The third occasion came after returning from a visit to Chile in 2018, a trip overshadowed by the clerical sexual abuse scandal.
“On one occasion, a few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice [his underlining], triumphant, possessing everything: ‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted,’” the pope wrote on January 24, 2021. “Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice. The Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and he thus freed me.”
Catholic teaching holds that the devil is a fallen angel and a real presence, and Catholic tradition cautions that those who are serious about attaining holiness will often encounter strong spiritual opposition. During his pontificate, Francis would frequently mention the devil, linking it to gossip and money. “The devil enters through the pockets,” he often said.
The diary also includes details of how Francis believed God spoke to him in dreams. On one occasion, Francis recounted seeing “the entrance to hell.” The pope, in 2018, described it as a form of “pagan seduction in full force,” an apparent reference to the worshipping of idols. “I peeked in to look a little and it terrified me. It was before going to sleep. I grabbed the rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help,” he wrote.
The book reveals that in 2021-2022, Francis underwent a spiritual crisis connected to a temptation or “curiosity” with power and which was partly connected to excessive activity and feelings of self-sufficiency. It was, the pope explained, also linked to “governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation.”
To counter the temptation, he sought to exercise greater humility and patience, even leaving people in place in the church’s central administration who others felt were undermining his papacy. During his 12-year pontificate, Francis, initiated several reforms in the church, including on the treatment of LGBTQ Catholics and the role of women, but faced significant opposition. Some of it came from inside the Vatican, where some bishops and cardinals openly resisted his reforms.
The Pope Francis I knew: Reflections from CNN’s Vatican correspondent
“One time in my presence, a bishop asked him why he had not yet fired someone in the Roman Curia who had been speaking badly of him in public and pursuing a personal agenda very different than his,” wrote Cardinal Fernández, who was appointed by Francis to lead the Vatican’s doctrine office. “After an interminable silence, he responded by explaining that he felt a strong sensation in his heart that God did not want him to become a puppeteer who uses and manipulates people according to his own convenience. He explained that, for this reason, he preferred to let that person remain in his position.”
While the diary doesn’t go into specific examples, the pope wrote on December 30, 2022, that he refused the temptation to treat “others like puppets.” In 2018, he said that “this sense of self-sufficiency and I can solve everything brought me to the gates of hell. I can’t forget the day I saw it.”
The crisis that Francis underwent, Fernández explained, was “connected to power” and the curiosity to “discover what it is like to exercise one’s own power.” As a member of the Jesuit religious order, the pope was continuously engaged in a spiritual discernment, essentially engaging in self-examination to determine whether he was working for self-interest or the good of others.
For Francis, feeling that he was “above the world” through his power was “the path of the worst spiritual worldliness imaginable, which he sought to dismantle by avoiding every symbol or expression of papal ‘majesty’ or ‘glory,’” Fernández added.
During his pontificate, Francis adopted a simple style, living in a Vatican guesthouse, wearing black orthopedic shoes and refusing certain papal vestments.
While the diaries focus on the pope’s spiritual life, they do include comments about the clerical sexual abuse crisis, including in Chile in 2018. At the time, Francis was criticized for dismissing the case of a bishop who had been accused of witnessing and covering up abuse when he was a priest. The pope later apologized for his handling of the case and summoned all the bishops from the country to Rome. In an unprecedented move, the bishops offered their resignations to the pope en masse .
“Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the airplane. I fell off the cot then,” Francis wrote. “It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn’t think it was so serious.” The phrase “fell off the cot,” the book explains, means to suddenly wake up to something. Francis would go on to make several reforms aimed at tackling clerical sexual abuse.
The diaries reveal the pope’s thoughts on Cardinal Robert Prevost, the future Pope Leo XIV, whom Francis brought to the Vatican to lead the department for appointing bishops. According to Fernández, Francis called Prevost “a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man.”
He was also generous to his critics, including Cardinals Robert Sarah, a Guinean, and Gerhard Muller, a German prelate. The Argentine pontiff said Sarah had “a refined spiritual sensitivity” and that Muller “seems aggressive but he’s a good man,” Fernández wrote.
The diaries reveal Pope Francis’ dedication to his ministry, frequently mentioning feelings of exhaustion, both in Argentina and after his election. Francis rarely took a day off and never went on vacation outside the Vatican. In 2019, he described himself as “feeling exhausted, almost without spiritual support and without a point of reference.”

articles.title_orig: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.title_zh: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.
"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.
The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.
The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.
Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.
The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.
To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.
"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said . "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."
Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon , an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.
Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.
"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.
OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.
"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."
"Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative ."

articles.title_orig: Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy
articles.title_zh: Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy
articles.content_orig:
For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.
Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation .
In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.
Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.
The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.
Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."
Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.
The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.
As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."
The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.
Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).
One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.
This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump . Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."
The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.
"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.
This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"
The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

articles.title_orig: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.title_zh: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.content_orig:
Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK
A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests , said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.
"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

articles.title_orig: Missile on truck in Llangollen goes viral on TikTok
articles.title_zh: Missile on truck in Llangollen goes viral on TikTok
articles.content_orig:
A 20ft-long Cold War era missile perched on the back of a truck in a field has become a hit on TikTok - and revealed a love story behind it.
Photos and videos of the striking sight near Llangollen, Denbighshire, spread across social media, prompting speculation, theories and curious comments from people wondering how it got there and why.
But for the man who owns it, the story has nothing to do with secret military operations or preparations for war - it is about him using an unusual hobby to honour his late wife.
Adrian Hyde, 59, admits it has now "all just snowballed and I've got carried away", and has spent about £200,000 on numerous vehicles.
Military enthusiasts Adrian and his wife Janette spent years talking about owning a military vehicle and planned to buy a tank as a joint 50th birthday present.
"We had all the area and ground ready, the driveway ready. We knew exactly where we were going to buy it from. We were going to buy a Russian one from Poland," said Adrian.
But this dream was put on hold when Janette was diagnosed with cancer in 2016.
Despite having cancer three times, Adrian said she never lost her determination and the couple "kept saying 'we'll eventually get that tank'. I think that's what kept us going".
Janette died in January 2025 at the age of 57, and Adrian found himself returning to their shared dream and bought the tank three months later.
"The first week after she passed, I said 'I'm going to get that tank she wanted'."
Adrian bought a CVRT scimitar and had it restored by "some military guys in Rugby" who made it road legal.
He named it Janbabes, after his wife.
Then, after getting a call from a military vehicles company telling him they had an armoured Land Rover, he bought that as well.
Adrian said word got round about his collection, leading to a call from a friend saying he had a 1957 AFS Bedford RL missile launcher and a Thunderbird missile for sale.
But because the driveway was full, he asked his friend John if he could put the missile launcher in his field, about 100 yards from his house and he said yes.
Adrian said the bug then got him and he bought a Special Forces Polaris 6 MRZR 4 , which is a project for next summer, with the collecting and restoration helping him cope with his grief.
"I'll be in the front room and look at the tank and think: 'That's part of you dear. That's Janbabes sitting there'."
The unusual sight quickly attracted attention locally before exploding online after a video posted by a hiker and content creator went "absolutely viral" on TikTok and Instagram.
Adrian said: "I've had people ringing me about it. I've got loads of people trying to get friendly on Facebook. It's gone crazy.
"To me it's natural, I have always grown up with military kit, but I suppose it is different."
He said many people have commented saying the missile was live, but that was "ludicrous".
"It's all inactive. It's from the 1950s but in mint condition," he said.
The Thunderbird was withdrawn from service in the 1980s, according to the Imperial War Museum.
"The missile is a Thunderbird missile from the Cold War era, but everything has been stripped off it.
"The inside is hollow. It's got the original outside shell but the inside all the electronics, explosives, jets, they've all been taken off and decommissioned."
A friend made the frame for it and bolted it on the back of a 1957 Bedford truck.
While many may see his military collection as odd, Adrian said it represented a dream he and Janette talked about for years, but never had the chance to realise together.
"It's quite emotional because it was our dream for 10 years. Janette would have loved it."
But the military equipment is not the only way Adrian has honoured his wife.
Following her death, he bought and donated an ambulance to cat charity Candy Tibby Trust in Wrexham, filling it with cat food and raising £3,000 in Janette's memory.
He hopes the sale of the missile and truck can do something similar as his wife was a cat lover.
As for what's next on the list, Adrian said he "doesn't know what yet".
"There are always plans to go buy something. It all depends on what crops up."
Whatever arrives next, its origins can be traced back to a husband keeping alive a dream he once shared with his wife.

articles.title_orig: Ousted leader Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on Dec. 16, spokesperson says
articles.title_zh: Ousted leader Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh from exile on Dec. 16, spokesperson says
articles.content_orig:
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson said, as the government said she can only return through extradition.
Hasina went into exile in August 2024 after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule.
She was later sentenced to death by a Bangladesh court in her absence for ordering the deadly crackdown on the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Announcing her plan to return on the anniversary of the end of her country’s 1971 liberation war with Pakistan , she urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her flight on the national airline.
“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement on Tuesday.
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, Prime Minister Rahman’s press secretary, told the Associated Press news agency that the government would stick to its position on Hasina’s extradition as a convict.
“My government’s stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
Hasina is expected to be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.
The judiciary had earlier said that Hasina would not be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline and there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.
The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced Hasina from power.
Hasina’s father led the war against Pakistan and after independence was the first leader of the new People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
He was killed in a military coup in 1975, along with most of his family members. Hasina and her younger sister survived as they were out of the country.

articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Imposes Sanctions on Megaspeed, Singaporean Firm at Center of Nvidia Scandal
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Monday added the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors.
The Singapore-based company was added to the Commerce Departmentâs entity list on Monday afternoon, plans that were first reported by Semafor.
The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
According to a filing from Commerceâs Bureau of Industry and Security posted to the Federal Register Monday afternoon, seven total entities were added to the list from Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including various affiliates of Megaspeed, MSFusion, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, and Swiftdata. âThese additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,â the filing reads. âThese entities will be added with a license requirement for all items subject to the [Export Administration Regulations] and licenses will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.â
Technology exports already en route to the targeted companies will be allowed to go through, the filing suggests.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the departmentâs entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huangâs relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list âfor monthsâ but that âCommerce holds the pen.â Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.
âThe Commerce Department placed Megaspeed on the Entity List. This makes it unlawful to export any US-origin goods, software, or technology to Megaspeed,â BIS spokesman Thomas Wackman told Semafor. âIt is also now unlawful to export advanced SI chips to Megaspeed, even if the chips are produced outside the United States. Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings.â

articles.title_orig: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.title_zh: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration .
The court on Monday upheld Denmark 's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration . The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.
The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.

Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU . Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.
In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.
"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.

Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.
The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.
According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Admitted To Additional Extramarital Affairs Before His Return
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Admitted To Additional Extramarital Affairs Before His Return
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares fell on Tuesday after the return of Jensen Huang as CEO sparked a massive rally on Monday.
Nvidia shares were down 3.9% in premarket trading as of 4:40 a.m. ET.
Other U.S. semiconductor stocks were also lower in premarket trading on Tuesday, with Micron , Marvell Technology , AMD and Arm all down over 3%.
Huang, who resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair, was reinstated on Monday. The stock closed 30% higher following the news.
The company's board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him.
President Donald Trump also claimed he was personally involved in Huang's return. The president told CNBC that he spoke with the chip maker's board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder.
"I made the deal," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers during an interview on "Squawk on the Street."
Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security.
"And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine."
After Huang's reinstatement, several Wall Street analysts turned more bullish on the stock and upgraded their ratings on Nvidia .
"We believe reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang RETURNS Investor CONFIDENCE in the AI trade," Mizuho analysts wrote in a note on Monday.
Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI story, supplying the chips that power AI and financing companies across the ecosystem.
The tech giant remains under scrutiny as questions remain about Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy.
The U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the company where she worked. There are also questions about whether Nvidia chips are making their way into China despite export controls.
Huang has been called to provide testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee next week. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to take over the Committee in January , called Huang's reinstatement "reckless."
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement on Monday.
Huang is also expected to answer questions from the House Foreign Affairs Committee next week.
"Reinstatement should not be confused with the end of scrutiny," Bank of America said in a note on Monday. "We therefore expect elevated attention around governance, China/export controls, customer relationships and compliance to persist even with the CEO question resolved."
— CNBC's Luke Fountain, Seema Mody and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon delays Patriot missile shipments to Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Pentagon delays Patriot missile shipments to Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States to approve the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles after a week of Russian attacks across 20 regions of the country, with the latest attack killing 15 people in Kyiv and the city of Zaporizhzhia.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russia launched about 2,700 attack drones, nearly 1,460 guided aerial bombs and 165 missiles over the past week. A significant share of the missiles were ballistic, he said, including some supplied by North Korea.
“Against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to understand the delays in the delivery of antiballistic systems to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine is short of US-made Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s partners had already paid for the missiles through a NATO-coordinated programme that funds purchases of US weapons for Kyiv. However, their delivery is still awaiting Washington’s approval.
On Monday, rescuers in Ukraine raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike, after overnight attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 14 people.
An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the capital, hit a five-storey building, causing part of it to collapse.
At least 10 people were killed in Dymer, Kyiv Governor Tymur Tkachenko wrote on Telegram on Monday.
One more person was killed when a strike set a home ablaze in the city of Bila Tserkva, also in the Kyiv region, Tkachenko said.
Three people were ⁠killed when a Russian drone struck a grocery store in the city of Vyshneve, southwest of Kyiv, on Sunday, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook, adding that 15 ⁠people were injured.
Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, said a man was killed overnight in Russian shelling in the city of Zaporizhzhia.
Also on Sunday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces struck a cargo ship northeast of Ukraine’s Black Sea port city of Odesa overnight.
The ministry said Russian drones also struck the Pravoberezhna electricity facility in Zaporizhzhia, which it said supplied power to Ukrainian arms manufacturers. It reported further strikes on an oil refinery, electrical substations and a data centre operated by MKM Telecom.
In its battlefield update, the ministry claimed Russian forces had taken control of the Ukrainian village of Sosnovyi Bir in the northeastern Kharkiv region and destroyed a launcher for Ukraine’s Neptune coastal missile system.
It also said it struck energy and transport facilities it described as serving Ukraine’s military. The Russian claims could not be independently verified.
